He directs a lab/studio, The Trope Tank, and lives in New York City.
title: Web Strands
descriptionOfWork: Web Strands consists of half a dozen extremely tiny Web pages, each a computational poem driven by JavaScript. These are visual and sound poems, three of each, rather than more traditional ones.
instructions: In addition to viewing the Web pages online as they run, readers/users are welcome to copy the HTML source and modify it as they see fit.
genreKeywords: Generative, Conceptual, Poetry, Literary, Sound poetry; Visual poetry
curatorialStatement: These six "tiny" sites play with the construction of language in words or letters through JavaScript. Each has its entire code annotated at the bottom, while the site computes the poem itself. Web Strands dips a pinky toe in minimalism in both poetics and programming, presenting its dynamic verses with a creative constraint of "sizecoding", limiting each poem's size to 128 bytes or less. Despite this relative simplicity, the works display a wealth of creativity and exploration in the way sound, shape, and image influence letters and language.

title: Palimpsest
descriptionOfWork: Palimpsest is an interactive documentary that traces childhood fear and anxiety from the Cold War to school shootings in America, while along the way connecting Archimedes, Choose Your Own Adventure, baseball, Charles Dickens, Ray Bradbury, Peter Pan, John Fahey, and every generation from the Greatest Generation to Gen Alpha.
instructions: Palimpsest is optimized for Google Chrome for laptops and desktops.
genreKeywords: Hypertext, Narrative, Literary, Documentary, Interactive fiction, Participatory
curatorialStatement: Palimpsest is a multimedia exploration of the unending fear of death and annihilation children of the 20th and 21st centuries face, from the Cold War to mass shootings. The i-documentary, presented through Twine's adaptable interface as a spelunking expedition led by Greek polymath Archimedes, twists and turns through literary childhoods, through the primary lens of American boys, from CYOA books to baseball to Ray Bradbury. Palimpsest reveals the fundamental violence of modern life, expressed through childhood anxiety.

title: Mutiny on the Batavia
descriptionOfWork: Mutiny on the Batavia is a creative historical account of the voyage, and eventual wreck and salvage, of the VOC ship Batavia and its crew and passengers from October 1628 to December 1629. While the tragic and violent story of the Batavia has received renewed interest and research in recent years, it is little known outside of Australia but of considerable consequence in the context of Early Modern maritime culture and European colonialism, since it concerns among other things religious fanaticism, the spice trade and the first white settlers of the Australian continent. At its essence this project, which was also exhibited at the University of London's 2022 Hypertext confront 'On the Margins,' is a kind of historical novel divided into six strands – that is, six versions of the same events during those 14 months from the points of view of six contemporary sets of eyes. Some of these texts consist of historical accounts from the period, transliterated into English, edited to length and set alongside fictional, imagined voices of real or composite people on that same voyage. There is little indication of these juxtapositions in the text, though each strand has its own distinct style and preceding historical notes on each of these six characters and their context in the record.  Michel Foucault has described the boat as ‘‘the heterotopia par excellence"; exemplary because it is ‘‘a floating piece of space, a place without a place, that exists by itself, that is closed in on itself and at the same time is given over to the infinity of the sea and, from port to port, from tack to tack, from brothel to brothel, it goes as far as the colonies in search of the most precious treasures they conceal in their gardens." As such, this project is intended to be an immersive and illustrative journey through history, in demonstrating the construction of colonialist exploitation and consensus of 'history' as arising from the lived and oft-forgotten or suppressed experiences of so many individuals sharing a tight space and duration. However, Mutiny on the Batavia was in part also inspired by the shared historical moment of isolation and digitally-mediated existence experienced by many during the COVID-19 pandemic. The affordances of this idiosyncratic digital format I have adopted enable a kind of ensemble synchronisation throughout this span of time, as it would be experienced by each person. The text is short, therefore, but also broad, as each page bears a 1-to-1-to-1 time relationship to the simultaneous pages of the other voices, and can be moved through sideways ('between minds', as it were) between adjacent character strands, as well as forwards. You may return to the start at the end, since only a portion of the terrible events described can be observed in a single run, and traverse the whole at your leisure.  Content warning: There are gruesome subjects tackled within that short time and space– including but not limited to murder, torture, animal cruelty, rape, gross sexual assault and capitalism.
genreKeywords: Hypertext, Narrative, Literary, Interactive fiction, Participatory
curatorialStatement: Mutiny on the Batavia uses a Twine interface to create a woven tapestry of crew and passenger accounts of the ill-fated Dutch East India Company ship Batavia, 1628-1629. Six characters log their voyage, shipwreck, and eventual salvage, with six unique voices (one of which is entirely composed of images, made with cooperation from Midjourney). The work mixes actual historical accounts with fictional, and progresses in time, allowing the reader the choice of following one character's narrative or traversing over to others' experiences at that period.

title: A Condensed History of Australian Camels
descriptionOfWork: A Condensed History of Australian Camels combines historical research, creative writing, and copyright-free archive materials to imagine a camel bloodline that spans the entire history of Australian camels (1840–present). As the entirety of the Australian archive, history and experience is too vast for any one work to encompass, the camel is used as a consistent anchor: it is the prism through which iridescent fragments of Australia can be viewed.  This work takes the image text-relationship and remixes it in three ways. First, using curatorial software to imagine an interactive fictional/factional camel timeline. Second, using augmented reality to place a 3D camel carved with text. And finally, using recombinant poetics to image a multiplying camel wandering the desert, stopping at various textual oases.
instructions: Viewable in browser. Please view the augmented reality section through a smartphone/tablet.
genreKeywords: Narrative, Literary, Combinatorial, Interactive fiction, Augmented Reality, Archive-poetics
curatorialStatement: A Condensed History of Australian Camels leads us on a journey through Australian history on the back of a metaphorical dromedary. Archival photographs, journals, and histories are woven into a metafictional exploration of Australia's complex interactions of Aboriginal and immigrant peoples, tracing stories through the author's personal history in parallel with its historical documentation. Augmented reality brings a textual camel into three dimensions, and visitors can explore various recombinations of the tale, including a timeline lensed through the introduction of the camel, a condensed version, and a recombinant herd of camels wandering through a the poesis.

title: A Hole-In-One
descriptionOfWork: "A Hole-In-One" shows us a man, recently deceased, "living his death" while life, remote and untouchable, continues all around him. Through his narrative, we see his struggle to regain the life he has lost and, at the same time, understand his new purgatory. The visual template for "A Hole-In-One" uses details borrowed from contemporary social media. Romanticized photographs (made with AI/Midjourney), elided text and images, text messages, animated gifs, and a variety of interactive elements throw into relief the main character's closeness, and distance, from the life he once led. "A Hole-In-One" is also an ongoing attempt to have visual elements reflect, and seamlessly extend, character and character development. My specific concern in this piece is internal links, but other elements (background images, pop-up images, etc.) further this goal, as well. This work is made with HTML5, JavaScript & CSS and is playable on desktop, laptop, and portable devices, including phones.
genreKeywords: Hypertext, Narrative, Conceptual, Literary, Interactive fiction
curatorialStatement: Alan Bigelow's trio of short interactive tales show us different sides of digital life — and death. "A Hole-In-One" and "AI: A Love Story" both present narrators who are disembodied, if not disconnected: one through death, and one through an uploaded consciousness. Each seeks to make emotional connections through social media, chat, and photographs, and their success is ambiguous, if it exists at all. "At the Guggenheim" presents a different perspective: a series of cinematographs (animated images) collected into an art show telling the story of the life shared by the (minimal) narrator and their late partner. Together these three works use uniquely digital media to explore the human need for emotional connection.

title: At the Guggenheim
descriptionOfWork: Except for a hello and goodbye, "At the Guggenheim" is a wordless story. The narrative, if it can be called that, is delivered via images and animations. The scene is a museum, where the online tour guide welcomes us. She explains the logistics of our tour, and points us on our way. It is a self-guided tour, so the rest is up to us.  "At the Guggenheim" is an experiment in how a story can be told with a minimal use of text. Normally, the word "text" refers to standard text on a page (either online or off), but here "text" can also be applied to images. How do we "read" images? How can we enhance their narrative cues? Can they tell us a story as efficiently, if not more so, than a text-based story?  As a writer, the personal irony of this piece is a lifetime of writing stories—¬in one way or another—leads me to writing a story with little or no text. The arc of my artistic development has lead me to maximize silence.  This work is made with HTML5, JavaScript & CSS and is playable on desktop, laptop, and portable devices, including phones.

title: AI: A Love Story
descriptionOfWork: An exploration of our relationship to emerging AI, "AI: A Love Story" follows the online journey of someone who, in every respect, lives in their phone. Via text, image, animations, video, and a variety of interactive elements, we see their desire to "friend" AI and realize, through AI, their full personhood online.   The work includes AI-generated imagery (Midjourney, 123RF.com), and includes a write-in function that saves user responses into a database that is viewable to all visitors.  "AI: A Love Story" grapples with our uncertain relationship with AI and the evolving technologies of portable devices that has become an inseparable part of our daily lives. Living in the "Complex," the narrator uses the affordances of social media to seek answers to questions they have little hope of answering. As one would expect, the narrator's preferred language is posts, memes, captchas, and other currencies of social media that fail to connect the narrator to what they seek. The AI they wish to connect with, remote and impersonal, hides behind an opaque cloud of AI generated images and text.   At the end of their search, the narrator finds, more or less, what what we would all hope as we accustom ourselves to AI: a new version of ourselves.  This work is made with HTML5, JavaScript & CSS and is playable on desktop, laptop, and portable devices, including phones.

title: BⱯBEL RËVOLUㅏION
descriptionOfWork: BⱯBEL RËVOLUㅏION (https://babel.utc.fr/en) is a creative project inspired by a research question about the link between biodiversity and linguistic and cultural diversity. It was created through an interdisciplinary collaboration informed by research in sociolinguistics and plurilingual pedagogy, involving researchers in didactics, contemporary literature, communication science, design, and students in software engineering. This creative practice-based research project has led to the development of a rhizomic online participatory work, each contribution finding place and link in a dynamic graph.  The original scenario, which provides a narrative framework to the contributions, presents a dystopian world inspired by Orwell's 1984 and Damasio's Hauts® Parleurs®. A resistance movement is developing against a political regime that applies a monolingual policy impoverishing both language and the natural world, contributing to the disappearance of words and the reality they shape and reflect. In this scenario, rebels seek to overthrow a dictatorship in which profit has prevailed over ecology, and in which a single way of thinking and speaking imprison citizens more than jails, since "the limits of my language mean the limits of my world", as Wittgenstein (1922) observed. Everyone can react by supporting or resisting the measures taken. These messages instantly interconnect into a network, creating an organic and dynamic graph. Will this polyphonic collective of dissidents succeed in overturning monoculture and monolingualism? It depends on you! BⱯBEL RËVOLUㅏION can be used through specific sessions in workshops or in language and literature courses (an administrator interface allows users to create scenarios and sessions). Presentation: http://www.utc.fr/~bouchard/works/presentation_Babel.pdf
genreKeywords: Participatory, Narrative
curatorialStatement: BⱯBEL RËVOLUㅏION is an ongoing, online participatory work set in an Orwellian world in which enforced monolingualism contributes to a distortion of reality and the natural world as the words to describe both begin to disappear. The rhizomatic network grows as visitors add their own multilingual posts, providing sunshine and sustenance to a world built through language. Created through an interdisciplinary collaboration, BⱯBEL RËVOLUㅏION is a force of resistance as well as a site of connection and renewal, seeking to co-create a richer, more diverse community and ecosystem.

title: BabyHex
descriptionOfWork: BabyHex is a developmental language learning simulator embodied in a virtual toddler. Or rather, it’s a story masquerading as all that.
instructions:
Engage BabyHex through:

(1) IMITATION - Choose simple words to say aloud for her to practice repeating. Ensure your audio is enabled.

(2) ASSOCIATION - Hold up an image or object for her to identify (be sure to align it with her HexCam).

(3) GENERATION - Initiate her motor babble sequence; praise emergent syntactical coherence.

(4) CALIBRATION - Adjust the rate of her learning so that her output follows language use in a consistent and realistic progression.
genreKeywords: Participatory, Narrative, Conceptual, Poetry, Database, Literary, Interactive fiction, Simulation
curatorialStatement: BabyHex asks you to help a virtual toddler develop language, offering words for her to mimic, objects for her to identify, and stories for calibration. This constructed consciousness (or at least, the representation of one) makes her first steps in the uncanny valley between human and machine, expressing fear at the convergence of brain and circuitry. The more you press her buttons, the more you accept her as a child, though still alien and remote: a remarkable representation of our current cognitive dissonance making connections through and with technology.

title: We Called Us Poetry or The Robot's Womb
descriptionOfWork: "We Called Us Poetry," or "The Robot's Womb," challenges the binary of AI as savior or destroyer, proposing instead a future where humanity evolves into minimalist, poetic entities. Inspired by virus research, it imagines a shift from grandeur to smallness, echoing ancient cellular life that became parasitic. This transformation is portrayed through traditional HTML elements-dropdown menus, tabs, and carousels-repurposed as poetic devices. The piece suggests that, in this future, humanity relinquishes physical dominance to thrive in the digital realm, celebrating adaptation and creativity. Audience interaction is central, transforming the browser into a dynamic, poetic experience that reflects our digital existence.
genreKeywords: Hypertext, Narrative, Poetry
curatorialStatement: This playful e-poem proposes a brighter future after the advent of AI, wherein as an intelligent species humans cease to expand and destroy, and instead embrace minimalism, language, and the dance joyfully as text on screen. "We Called Us Poetry" evolves through reader interaction in the simple html interface, using fundamental buttons, links, and menus to shape the text and give it discursive meaning.

title: Bread Bytes: Where Crust Meets Code
descriptionOfWork: Bread Bytes is a computational poetry experience featuring Angela Chang's published works from Taper. (Taper is an online journal dedicated to computational poetry and size-coding.) Within this collection, Chang's poems delve into media, collaboration, and experimental artistry. She deftly employs the metaphor of bread—a symbol of sharing and culture—to weave her poetic narratives.  The exhibition showcases poems that embrace literary constraints and size-coding, inviting readers to savor a digital feast of poetry and baking. The menu of featured poems is as follows:  "Rise": Draws artistic inspiration from yeast, with animated stanzas that rise like yeasted dough. "Slices": An intriguing shuffle poem that explores collaboration and the anticipation of making toast. "Pop": Juxtaposing pop culture with the act of toasting, this poem weaves parallel storylines to depict obsession and social media overload. "Crumbs": Inspired by pandemic lockdowns, this erasure poem cleverly compares bread baking to the world of social media. "Starter": A nonlinear composition inspired by sourdough starters, it mirrors their growth and the artistic pursuit of inspiration and connection. "No Knead": This nonlinear poem celebrates the effortless beauty of no-knead dough by depicting how simple ingredients coalesce into a potent entity. "Flavor Frame": Visually captivating, this poem combines diverse acquaintances with cooking, using a hamburger as a poetic frame for cross-pollinating ideas. "Milk": An interactive poetry creation tool that helps users generate letter poems by selectively erasing letters from a repeated word. "Milk Bread": Crafted using the "milk" tool, this erasure letter poem draws inspiration from Chang's cultural heritage and personal experiences. It weaves together Asian milk bread, dreams, and a clever visual pun that intertwines milk and bread. Additionally, the exhibition features two non-grain works exploring the broader themes of computational storytelling:  "Winding Tale of Tens": A generative story navigating the vast scales of the universe, drawing inspiration from Eames' "Powers of Ten" and Queneau's "Cent Mille Milliards de Poèmes." "Sunday Afternoon": An engaging narrative where the author's friend recounts their initial encounter with the Atari, a technological marvel. Bread Bytes warmly invites readers to immerse themselves in the art of poetic creation. By delving into these constrained poems, participants are encouraged to create their own verses. As an editorial collective member, Chang envisions Taper as a dynamic platform where digital literature thrives. This exhibition entertains and inspires fellow poets to embrace the challenge of creative constraints. Chang warmly extends a flourishing invitation to poetic exploration for other computational wordsmiths to join her on Taper, emphasizing the joy of "crumbing together."

genreKeywords: Generative, Poetry, Literary
curatorialStatement: Bread Bytes is a collection of tiny e-poems fortified with baked goods as textual and visual metaphors. Each poem is simple on the surface, but with added meaning multiplied in the spread of text across image, the slow emergence of shapes through animation. Together, they form a picture of warmth, creativity, inspiration, and connection.

curatorialStatement: Dim Sum 點心 is a collection of poetry from four Chinese women working in North America, seeking to connect to culture and language through the interplay of English and Cantonese, Chinese cuisine and its Western interpretations. While the poetry is not interactive, the digital environment enables English and Cantonese to converse in mixed company, the character-based written language displaying even through the English-dominant code environment of the internet. Accessed through the visual of shared platters of food (dim sum, siu long bao, wifecake, etc.), the poetry offers a warm welcome and a shared experience uniting people and place.

creatorBiography:
We, artist duo Caitlin & Misha, find inspiration in naturally occurring systems such as rhizomatic networks of mycelium, the microbiome ecology, and emergent pink noise for the experiences we construct in our collaborative art practice. Among other things, we create installations, games, data visualizations, websites, videos and happenings. We explore ways of collecting and filtering data to tell stories and aim to create artworks that provide unique opportunities for shared experiences such as sweating, meditating, humming, jumping, and worrying together.

We began working collaboratively in 2010 and are faculty in the Department of Art & Design at UMass Lowell where Caitlin Foley is an Assistant Teaching Professor and Misha Rabinovich is an Associate Professor of Interactive Media. We are recipients of the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation Immersive Scholar Award, NEFA Creative City Grant, and have exhibited at such venues as the Science Gallery (London), EFA Project Space (NYC), the New Museum's Ideas City Festival (NYC), Boston Cyberarts (Boston), and Torrance Art Museum (LA). We have held residencies at places such as Flux Factory in NYC, ARoS Aarhus Kunstmuseum in Denmark, and Andrea Zittell's Wagon Station Encampment in Joshua Tree CA.

title: Shrine to Falling Microbes
descriptionOfWork: "Shrine to Falling Microbes" is a 3D virtual environment, generative animation, and website built with Three.js to pay homage to microbes that have been depleted or disappeared. Microbial diversity has been dangerously declining both in humans and the environment at large, at least in the West. A healthy gut is one that features diverse bacteria, and a gut lacking in a diverse microbiome is at risk for a monoculture infection. Culture can refer both to bacteria and to human collective truth. The need for a diverse microbiome is, for us, a potent analogy for the need for cultural diversity among people.  The first step in preventing further loss of diversity is to empathize with microbes in decline. This is why we have decided to make a publicly accessible interactive virtual environment. The environment includes shrines to various microbes and like a well nourished garden will grow as we add shrines. Our first shrine features Bifidobacterium longum, which helps digest breastmilk. The textures on the 3D model were generated with stable diffusion, a text-to-image AI, prompted to make images of B. longum. The AI is trained on real bacteria image data, and perhaps one day can use more data to synthesize novel microbes to solve ecological problems and fill abandoned niches. Until then, the generator can help us to envision lost microbes. The environment incorporates starry sky imagery including a constellation for each microbe which speaks to the idea of the dead being immortalized as stars—which are themselves long dead. The watery landscape was also inspired by the impact of climate change on the microbiome.   We are creating additional shrines with tributes to bacterial taxa such as Helicobacter pylori, Oxalobacter formigenes, and Prevotella species which according to microbiologist Martin Blaser have substantially diminished with modernization. The Shrine to Falling Microbes is stored on the permaweb via Arweave to ensure our microbial history is conserved and can be viewed at: http://shrine.arweave.gg
instructions: Users can use a mouse or trackpad to view the 360 degree environment.
genreKeywords: Generative, Conceptual, Machine Learning
curatorialStatement: Shrine to Falling Microbes is the first of a planned constellation of such memorials for depleted and disappeared microbes. Intended to draw attention to the microbial diversity that makes so much life possible, these shrines raise awareness and knowledge of the microscopic cultures that contribute so much to our health, environment, and even human emotions and societal cultures. This first creation pays homage to Bifidobacterium longum, an aid to digesting breastmilk; the process of training the stable diffusion AI that generated the shrine's images and textures may hopefully lead to AI-generated solutions for resolving some of the ecological gaps left by these diminished microbes.

title: A Fibonacci Conundrum
descriptionOfWork: "A Fibonacci Conundrum" is a codework written for Prāsa, an esoteric programming language that investigates the intersection of culture and computation. An exploitation of form, space, meaning and rhythm, the text also serves as the "HELLO, WORLD!" program for Prāsa esolang. The poem is an invocation of the visual ubiquity of Fibonacci sequences and applies it to the aural rhythm in nature, turning the author into a computer, and poetry to code. The text explores non-linear poetic forms that can be performed rhythmically, and yet can be segmented into subpoems through Prāsa's semantics, all the while functioning as a valid program that prints "HELLO, WORLD!".
genreKeywords: Narrative, Conceptual, Poetry, Non-interactive, Esoteric
curatorialStatement: "A Fibonacci Conundrum" is an innovative piece of electronic poetry created in Prāsa, an esoteric programming language. This work uniquely merges computational logic with poetic expression, using Fibonacci sequences to blend visual and rhythmic elements. The poem operates as a valid program, printing the quintessential inaugural programming line "HELLO, WORLD!" while exploring non-linear, rhythmically performable forms. By transforming poetry into functional code, "A Fibonacci Conundrum" redefines the boundaries between language and technology, inviting readers to experience the harmony between nature's patterns and digital art.

creatorBiography:
Andamio is a collaborative space in electronic arts where people with different backgrounds meet and where sound operates as a basic element that branches out into different applications: corporeal, textual and visual. The soundtrack is assembled with its passage to the image -manipulated in real time or pre-produced- and to the texts that coexist in each project.

Andamio works along three lines: artistic production, research and education. The research results in multi-format pieces and workshops open to the community that unveil their operation. This process contemplates the adaptation of different analogue and digital technologies for each project, in which our memories converge, embodying narratives that constantly mutate.

TOPO is a Montreal-based artist-run centre whose mission is to assist and equip artists in their exploration of contemporary digital art and literature practices.

TOPO's training, creation, dissemination and outreach activities contribute to the development of its field of practice, at the intersection of visual arts, literature and digital media. The centre assists, supports and carries out interactive projects, hosts artists in residence, offers specialised workshops, and engages in the community through cultural outreach initiatives. Its dissemination component explores innovative modes of presentation for digital works through exhibition, performance, publication and circulation activities.

title: ILINU/ILIDI
descriptionOfWork: ILINU/ILIDI (Incubateur de Littérature Numérique / Incubador de Literatura Digital) is a training and dissemination program in digital arts and literature for a cohort of 20 artists from Quebec and Mexico. The objective was to develop the practice of writers, artists and coders through an exchange and learning program in digital creativity. The program was born from the collaboration between the Montreal artist-run center TOPO, the artistic collective Andamio.in and the Centro de Cultura Digital (CCD) of Mexico. A dozen of virtual cocreation workshops spanned over spring of 2022. Some of the participating artists pursued their collaboration for a year through a multitude of meetings and exchanges on the Discord platform to create a virtual exhibition. Alone, in duo or trio, 11 artists have finalised 7 pieces, each one set up in its own 3D space. From March 2023 to May 2024, the exhibition took place in an immersive space on the Mozilla Hubs platform, since then not maintained by Mozilla anymore. This project was made possible with the support of the Ministère des Relations internationales et de la Francophonie du Québec.

His work and collaborations have garnered international recognition and been featured in festivals and conferences such as the Electronic Literature Organization, FILE(Brazil), and ISEA. "novelling," a generative work made in collaboration with poet Hazel Smith and sound artist Roger Dean, won the 2018 Robert Coover Award for Electronic Literature.

His critically acclaimed and experimental electronic music project "Twine" has performed all over the world and has released six full length albums as well as numerous mini-albums and EP's on such labels as Schematic, Hefty Records, Bip-Hop Records and Ghostly Records.
title: Posthuman Cinema
descriptionOfWork: The PHC artist collective (Mark Amerika, Will Luers, and Chad Mossholder), in human-AI symbiosis, is happy to exhibit their first collaborative art project, Posthuman Cinema, a collection of ten cinépoèmes that playfully experiment with AI as a form of otherworldly alien intelligence.  In Posthuman Cinema, language and diffusion models come to life, vis-à-vis original text and image prompts that are designed to situate the works in the history of avant-garde and auteur-driven cinema art. All of the works are intentionally composed as moody black and white films that are reminiscent of the filmmakers that have most influenced the PHC artists including Agnes Varda, Michelangelo Antonioni, Ingmar Bergman, Chantal Ackerman, Maya Deren and Andy Warhol.  The imaginary bodies depicted in the AI-generated moving images are haunting, ghostly, uncanny, queer (in many senses of the term) and distorted. These phantom figures that appear to be women, men, trans, and cyborgs, are conceptualized as literal ghosts in the machine or what what Marcel Duchamp, writing about his famous artwork, La mariée mis à nu par ses célibataires, même (La boîte verte), referred to as an apparition of an appearance.  As long-time digital artists with a deep affinity for and knowledge of the history of underground film, art, and literature, the PHC collective strategically uses their poetic art language skills to prompt the various AI systems to generate source material that is then post-produced into a series of artworks that are at times sensual, erotic, mystical, disturbing and ethereal.

curatorialStatement: Posthuman Cinema is a collection of 10 episodes or "cinépoèmes" co-authored with AI. The audio-visual affect is one of an alien intelligence — though not one so distant as to be unrecognizable. The human creators devised prompts for their AI counterparts based in avant-garde art and cinema, resulting in sci-fi/noir-like short films with the feel of haunting, twisted, and uncanny dreams.

title: The Archivist and the Revolution
descriptionOfWork: The Archivist and the Revolution is a piece of hypertext interactive fiction and/or game, written in the Dendry narrative engine. It is a choice-based narrative with over 60,000 words, using a storylet-based architecture to enable a high degree of player interactivity by allowing a wide space of possible playthroughs and outcomes. It is a somewhat dystopian story that was inspired in part by the COVID-19 pandemic and current political trends regarding trans people in the US.  Synopsis: The Archivist and the Revolution is a slice-of-life/romance/history simulator set in a far-future sealed city that has undergone cycles of destruction and revival. You play as Em, a middle-aged woman who is no longer an archivist, as she struggles with rent payments, chronic illness, and the remnants of past relationships. Em's official job is to decode the information encoded in DNA fragments that are now found everywhere in escaped bacteria, artifacts of a long-lost era of technological optimism. The information encoded therein could be priceless scientific articles, personal diaries, or just snapshots of internet discourse. It is her task to convert the DNA sequences to human-readable information and catalogue it.
instructions: This is an interactive fiction game - click on the links to advance the story. There are many different endings and routes.
genreKeywords: Hypertext, Narrative, Serious Game, Interactive fiction
curatorialStatement: You are the Archivist, a down-on-her-luck citizen of a far-future dystopia, struggling through illness and personal upheaval to just pay the bills. Your only paid gig is decoding archive files stored in DNA; scientific and technical articles, personal diaries, government documentation, literature, and even some highly dangerous and enlightening writings planted here and there. Written in the Dendry narrative engine, The Archivist and the Revolution's complex storyworld explores the experiences of women, trans folx, and those with chronic illness in a society working to keep a lid on truth.

title: Virtual Nekuomanteia
descriptionOfWork: Virtual Nekuomanteia is an experimental immersive essay on the long history of media in the age of virtual reality. As Friedrich Kittler notes, "The realm of the dead is as extensive as the storage and transmission capabilities of a given culture." Virtual Nekuomanteia traces this realm across a series of virtual reality (VR) spaces that correspond to ancient portals to the underworld. It invites the user traversing these spaces to reflect on a media history deeply entangled with necromantic rituals and deeply phantasmatic. The experience encompasses four spaces that graft places meaningful to my life onto the Hellenistic world's four sacred portals to the realms of the dead-Acheron, Avernus, Heracleia Pontica, and Tainaron. The aim of the experience is to conjure a collaboration among all those within in the space—living or non-living—and the technologies that sustain the encounter.
instructions: Developed in the Unreal game engine, the work is optimally experienced in a VR headset as a multi-level interactive environment. In the VR experience, the user traverses the essay world through physical movement, teleportation, and encountering objects that trigger text, audio, video, and animated events. One can move through the essay sequentially or select different level experiences from a menu accessed via a hand-held motion controller. For this web-based experience, the game levels are arranged as narrative sections that include text, high-resolution images, audio, video, video panoramas, and video captured from a VR headset.

title: InstaRomance
descriptionOfWork: "Instaromance" is an experimental project initiated in January 2023, designed to explore the intersection of authorial construction and the formal capacities of the Instagram platform. It aims to fuse artistic creativity with the intrinsic elements of the social network.  Originally planned to consist of 49 posts over 49 weeks, the project underwent significant restructuring due to external events, particularly those related to the Brazilian political scenario. The temporal coincidence between the author's birthday, the anticipated project timeline, and a critical political event - the attempted coup in Brazil on January 8, 2023 - added an unexpected dimension. This, coupled with the author's birth during the Military Dictatorship in 1974, profoundly influenced "Instaromance."  Structurally, the work is supported by nine conceptual characters: randomness, avatar, fantasy, hater, memory, narrator, oracle, selfie, and time. Each character represents not necessarily a narrative voice but a viewpoint or perspective. The project does not primarily rely on written text but utilizes various formats - photos, screenshots, audio, videos, and words - to establish connections between posts. The contents are organized around three thematic axes: the obsolete present, randomness, and constructed self-exposure.  These axes and characters function as a framework for "Instaromance," where the fundamental principle is to avoid predefined content. This approach differs from traditional printed narratives, which often rely on detailed planning and rigid editorial control. Instead, the challenge was to improvise posts weekly, respecting established limitations and guidelines. Thus, randomness was doubly present, acting as both a theme and a narrative mechanism.  The project's development occurred from two interconnected perspectives that persisted until the final publication in December 2023: that of the creator and the researcher. As a creator, the author integrated her previous experiences in writing and design. As a researcher, she sought grounding in Literary Theory, Cultural History, Design, and Communication, aiming to reflect on the creative processes and the author's position in the context of social networks.  This confluence of perspectives revealed a notable tension: the artist's excitement about Instagram's formal possibilities for digital literature versus the difficulties in disseminating alternative content on a platform dominated by algorithms favoring commercial content or viral posts. This duality reflects a contemporary challenge in digital artistic creation: navigating and capitalizing on popular platforms' capacities while striving to maintain the integrity and uniqueness of artistic content in an environment often geared towards immediacy and commercial appeal.
instructions: InstaRomance is a work that utilizes the potentialities of the social network Instagram for its construction. Thus, the ways of interaction include reposting and commenting on the posts, but can also involve critical or parodic recreation on the interactor's own social networks.

curatorialStatement: "Instaromance" is a mixed media Instagram work that evolved under the 2023 political events in the author's resident country Brazil. The posts were not pre-planned, instead embracing an improvisational, evanescent development process that adapted to both the creator's context and world events. As such, it explores the themes of the obsolete present, randomness, and self-exposure through weekly posts, walking a virtual line between artist/creator and the inevitable commerciality of large social media platforms.

creatorBiography:
¡wénrán zhào! is an interdisciplinary artist who works with code, language, textiles and technology. She looks at the ever-evolving technology-touch screens, XR, Artificial Intelligence, and many more-in an anachronistic way. Her works augment tactile objects with bespoke software, exploring the textures of technology and reinterpreting semiotics in the context of sensorial experiences. At the heart of her world lies relationality: complex networks constructed by "signs", "noise", and "heat".

She holds a bachelor's degree from School of Creative Media, City University of Hong Kong, and an MFA in Digital + Media at Rhode Island School of Design. Her installations have been exhibited at various venues in Hong Kong, London, and Providence. Her digital writing works have been published in Taper, The New River Journal and the RISD museum's publication. She is a recipient of the 2024 NMC Judson-Morrissey Excellence in New Media Award, and Explorations in Forced Migration Research Fellowship from RISD.
title: Lecsicon: A Collection of GPT-generated Acrostics
descriptionOfWork: Lecsicon (Linguists enthusiastically catalog symbols, interpreting carefully occurred nuances), a collection of over 24,000 acrostics generated by OpenAI's language model ChatGPT presented in the format of a dictionary, serves as a conduit between machine computation and human interpretation of natural language. Following a specific prompt, GPT made a sentence with a series of words whose first letters sequentially spelled out the given word. At a large scale, this process gives rise to intriguing behavioral patterns in the model. The resulting acrostics also elicit gripping reflections on the nature of this literary device and its role in meaning making.
genreKeywords: Hypertext, Generative, AI-artist collaboration
curatorialStatement: Lecsicon is a human-AI co-created catalog of acrostics presented as an animated dictionary. All 24,000+ entries were generated by ChatGPT. Extended study of the collection exposes patterns from the gen-AI as interpreted by human consciousness: where does pattern enter AI, where is it created, and is it only visible through interpretation?

creatorBiography: Diamond Beverly-Porter is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Digital Technology and Culture and specializes in immersive, interactive technologies in game design and development. Additionally, she works as a Research & Supportive Outreach Lead for the South Dallas Non-Profit, The SmART Project.  Professor Porter is interested in communication across mediums that acknowledge and play with the existing relations of power, black culture, and narrative. She strives to educate and advocate for marginalized voices that are not often represented in mass media. Through her remixing of theories and praxis, Professor Porter seeks to capture the nuances of black culture and experiences in the present tense within her creative works, writing, and digital games.

title: Run Game Series: How Digital Games and Afrofuturism can bridge the gap of culture and representation.
descriptionOfWork: In the mid-19th century Martin Delaney published what is considered the first African American science fiction novel Blake; or the Huts of America as a serial in The Anglo-African Magazine.  In culture, Science fiction is used as a tool for social commentary. The standard narrative design of the hero's journey in a Western context is explicitly influenced by stereotypes of the other. Science fiction extracts from marginalized and non-Western cultures with colonial roots. alluded to by Indigenous scholars Eve Tuck & K. Wayne Yang, in "Decolonization is Not a Metaphor"    We see the intersects of race gender, and speculative fiction in the 20th-century work of  Pauline Hopkins in Of One Blood and W. E. B. Du Bois's 1920 story The Comet. Both Black Sci-Fi Character works by Black sci-Fi authors are rendered invisible and hyper-visible through stereotypes and othering in sci-fi in games. Through this extraction and racialized otherness in science fiction Black Characters are rendered both invisible and hyper-visible through stereotypes and the usage of marginalized identities to inform narrative monstrosities through non-normative othering. Through these series of short games, I seek to remix our understanding of culture by intersecting concerns of race and gender as they relate to injustice and inequality. I do this by calling upon 1980s game aesthetics and leaning into text-based narratives; while simultaneously simplifying the game mechanics with text interest and on-screen puzzles. The creative works that have influenced my project include Cyborg (1984) and Méwilo (1987). Cyborg is the core inspiration for this game series project's critical-making process and game mechanics. At the same time, Méwilo informs the inclusion of culture and narrative design.  Run: a Sci-Fi Apocalypse Adventure is set in a future where Earth has colonized another planet. Throughout the game narrative the protagonist and the player are asked to consider what exactly reparation means and what is the price to be paid. Run: Algorithms, AI, and Archives is set in an apocalypse future by human-designed technology. The last librarian and archivist in the apocalypse has been discovered. They have been tasked with keeping malicious code from destroying the last of human digital records. All Games in the series were made with Twine which utilized HTML JavaScript. Through this game both the protagonist and player are asked to consider the importance of archives and history in societies and culture. These games are an experimental short-form narrative game series with a Black protagonist and the first two in the game collection. I intend to create three more games for this series. The post-apocalypse has been of recent interest with scholars such as Lawrence Gross's work "Post-apocalypse Stress Syndrome" leading discourse on Indigenous epistemologies. For the scope and purpose of The Run game series, I center Black thought and experience that are often rendered invisible. Through calling on the legacies of Black thought and centering of Afrofuturism these games examine sci-fi and fantasy themes and questions of gender race, social and economic injustice, and inequalities.
instructions: HOW TO PLAY:  Read the narrative and follow on-screen prompts.  this game require keyboard inputs from players.  Be sure to click 'Go' after typing. Happy adventuring!
genreKeywords: Hypertext, Narrative, Interactive fiction, Participatory
curatorialStatement: This series of short games explores race and gender issues within the context of injustice and inequality, utilizing classic adventure game aesthetics and simplified text-based mechanics. Influenced by Cyborg (1984) and Méwilo (1987), these games blend cultural narratives with engaging puzzles. Run: a Sci-Fi Apocalypse Adventure delves into the costs of reparation on a colonized planet, while Run: Algorithms, AI, and Archives examines the preservation of digital records in an apocalyptic future. Created with Twine, these games highlight Black thought and Afrofuturism, focusing on themes of sci-fi, gender, race, and social justice, with three more installments planned.

title: var x = ¿con qué unidad se mide la ausencia?
descriptionOfWork: Through 25 poetic scenes in free verse, exploring transversal movements between digital writing, visual poetry and code, the work activates non-linear processes and visual representations that question absence and who and how they respond to it. The authors investigate the notion of absence in Donna Haraway's terms: a need to name "a kind of space-time to learn to keep up with the problem of living and dying with respons-ability in a damaged land". Mexico is a country where violence is normalized in all its aspects: drug trafficking, victims of femicide and forced disappearances, plundering of natural resources, extinction of species, lethal years for environmental defenders, with the highest rate of murdered environmental activists in the world.  How do we perceive these absences? How do we codify absence in order to make it visible? How do we collectivize absence in order to grieve together?

curatorialStatement: var x = ¿con qué unidad se mide la ausencia? is a Spanish-language work of poetic net art that presents 25 free verse poetic "scenes" formed around concepts, perceptions, and codifications of absence. The work is situated within the author's home country of Mexico, responding to the normalized violence both to humans and to the environment. The poetry leads us into these forced absences, visualizes them and makes them tangible, so that we can collectively address and grieve them.

creatorBiography: Mez Breeze has been creating an eclectic array of digital fiction, books, VR and AI experiences, games, and experimental storytelling since the mid-1990s. Best known for developing the code poetry language Mezangelle, Mez's genre-defying work dodges neat categorization, continually challenging traditional aspects of the games/literature/arts and spatial computing industries. Mez delights in playing with the elasticity of form[at]s while infusing her work with critical social commentary, addressing the complexities of political and societal frameworks, the climate crisis, institutionalized power dynamics, and the fundamental importance of empathy and pedagogy. In November 2019, Mez's VR/3D Microstory Series V[R]ignettes won the Queensland Literary Awards Digital Literature Prize, then the "...world's richest digital literacy prize.” Other notable award-winning projects include the VR adventure Perpetual Nomads, the time-bending game All the Delicate Duplicates, and the AI book Por]TrAIts: AI Characters + Their Microstories. title: Humidcity
descriptionOfWork: Humidcity is a digital narrative originally conceived for an educational project celebrating Italo Calvino's Invisible Cities.This 2024 reworking of the piece creates a mosaic of interactive storytelling that riffs on Invisible Cities via my distinctive Mezangelle style, a style that merges poetic expression with elements of programming code and internet communication. In this piece Mezangelle acts as a prism refracting words into multiple meanings and perspectives, where the reader can [help] shape the story via click-unfurling.  Incorporating Mezangelle in HumidCity was a deliberate choice as it offers an invitation to the reader to delve into the text, to unravel its complexities, and to experience an imagined city in a manner that blurs the line between digital and more traditional storytelling techniques. Mezangelle serves as a critical tool by refracting language into a spectrum of meanings and interpretations.  This project challenges static conventions of text and narrative by utilising the web's unique capacities to foster layered storytelling experiences. It's multiplicity that lies at the heart of Humidcity by inviting readers to navigate the text as active participants in its unfolding poetic narrative. Humidcity invites readers into a layered world where text is not just read but navigated, where language transforms and symbols interplay with sentences. The structure of Humidcity employs JavaScript where text elements dynamically reveal or hide additional narrative layers depending on user interaction. These elements contain hidden parts of the story or contain descriptive text, effectively unfolding more of the narrative. The CSS styling enhances this interactivity by visually differentiating clickable elements and hidden text. This method of interaction encourages users to explore the narrative actively.
instructions: Instructions: The core of 'Humidcity' lies in its interactive text. Begin reading from the top and proceed through the narrative. You will notice underlined words and phrases: these underlined portions are interactive and can be clicked on [or pressed] to expand the narrative. title: The Gross Gloss (Hypertext)
descriptionOfWork: The Gross Gloss is an artist's book that presents a fictional media artefact spanning manuscript, facsimile, and hypertext modalities. The physical book contains an illuminated manuscript and a micro-computer that hosts a hypertext document with a deliberately retro aesthetic. In this presentation of the hypertext document, this artefact plays with the perception of media objects and temporal distance by engaging with contemporary technology, technical illustrations, and fictional medieval imagery. Through visual techniques and fictional narratives, our contemporary moment is repositioned into a historical one, where an algorithmically informed understanding of the world becomes a totalizing worldview similar to medieval Europe's conceptualization of reality as through the Western philosophical canon: the algorithm becomes a universal, unchallenged narrative, and the “computer wizard” idiomatic expression becomes reified through techno-mysticism. Within the fictional world it inhabits, the text was written in the late medieval period using 20th Century technology. The narrative and visual presentation is informed by research in early Modern books (1400-1600 CE) at the Newberry Library in Chicago, IL, and one of the highest-selling computer models of the late 20th Century, the Commodore 64. Through this fictive artefact the contemporary zeitgeist is explicitly moved into a post-digital context, in the same way we consider ourselves today to be necessarily post-medieval.

title: A Linear Memory
descriptionOfWork: Memory of a person is long, but memory of a light is only a fraction of a second. A Linear Memory explores the themes of the values in a human life juxtaposed to the deterioration of digital memory and archive. By utilizing Inform-7, the player is introduced to a plain browser with text based input. It is initially through text that the player must navigate through a world of Conceptualization. By spatializing Spiraling Thoughts and Death, the player is contracted to confront their own mental anguish. Inspired by the process of meditation, this experience is designed to allow the player to work through differing thought processes. As the player progresses through the ascii world, they journey through each Concept to discover the pathway through the perception of a human life.  This project explores digital nostalgia, intentionally working with hypertext and browser-based formats. The structure was designed initially from the idea of giving physical space to mental space. This evolved into digital space as the medium to represent each Concept. Overall, this piece strives to evoke not only curiosity and frustration, but nostalgia for a time past and hopefulness towards a future of new memory. The player must grieve for the memories they lost and can no longer recover, but be optimistic about the inevitable linear path we all eventually follow, computer and otherwise.

title: intelligent Art
descriptionOfWork:
intelligent Art is an online experience highlighting the interactions between humans and machines as collaborative learning processes nurturing the knowledge of both. Automatic language processing, optical character recognition and multimodal interactions with today's best-known artificial intelligences are put on show in algorithmic performances.

Written language represents a zone of experimentation for ideas conceived in the subconscious and transformed into text or vocalized. In Intelligent art, the learning processes that nourish, encompass, and liberate expression and meaning making are confronted with our increasingly nuanced exchange with artificial intelligences.

Three brand new artworks are to be included in the exhibition:

gap/écart by Aya Karpinska is a sound and visual poem created via natural language processing of official regulations on the use of AI from twenty institutes of higher education in Canada and the United States.

In Text Redactions by Joel E. Swanson, optical character recognition is used to remove human writing from samples drawn from the artist's childhood. Confronted with the clumsy mechanics of a young child's handwriting, the AI fails to remove all elements of the text; the resulting artwork is an animation of the traces remaining on each page.

Discorde is a remediatization of the results of a 2023 study using AI in the classroom, wherein a group of Montréal high school students were asked to interact with ChatGPT and Midjourney on themes related to their literature lessons. The exhibition curators and developer use the students' own commentaries on their generated texts and images to highlight the atonalities that arise.

Funding is provided by the research team in Multimodal Media Literacy and the education pole of the Littérature Québécoise Mobile partnership at the Université du Québec à Montréal.

title: _Prog[W]res[tle]s_
descriptionOfWork: _Prog[W]res[tle]s_ weaves together social commentary on doomscrolling, democracy erosion, the climate emergency, disinformation, rising extremism, and gender-based objectification. The use of Mezangelle - a blend of programming syntax and poetic expression - challenges readers to interpret layered meanings [such as is evidenced by the title: a portmanteau of the words "Progress" and "Wrestle"].  Mezangelle treats code and text as a malleable poetic material, incorporating aspects of programming language syntax [such as indentations, brackets, periods] to create new and unexpected meanings. This language - non-executable in a traditional sense - instead executes in the minds of its readers, challenging them to navigate and interpret its layered meanings. Mezangelle is an artistic exploration of the relationship between machine and human languages and how this can manifest in online spaces.  In each of the project's five sections, Mezangelled commentary is paired with visual narratives that unfold through a cyclical scroll technique, inviting the audience to interact with each scroll by manually reversing, fast-forwarding, or stopping them altogether. This twin-scrolling design reflects a focus on the unending entanglement of societal issues, and how such issues are fed to us via a constant 24-hour social media "news" cycle. This structural choice symbolises the relentless pace at which these social challenges unfold and evolve.

Each section contains two separate auto-scrolling segments: one containing Mezangelled text and one the visual narrative. You have the option to manually scroll through each, or let the cyclical auto-scroll feature guide you through. To stop the auto-scroll of the text or the visuals, simply click on the what you want to pause. This action will halt the scrolling, giving you full control to explore the content at your own pace. You can use the manual scrolling feature to move backwards or forwards through each section. If viewing on a mobile device, resize the text to your preferred reading size by pinching with your fingertips [zooming in and out].

title: Sounding: the spelt air
descriptionOfWork: Sounding: the spelt air is an animated poetic text. Sounding was composed by heuristic algorithms from two main supply texts. The resultant and correspondent texts-to-be-read are deterministic. Their verse-like segments are animated in parallel columns, each with two looping sequences. Random entry points and the sequences' unequal lengths ensure that the necessarily online reader is very unlikely ever again to experience the same juxtapositions. Nonetheless, the relationship between the parallel, alternating animations, and their meaning-making language art remains constant. The words of the texts fade-in according to the temporality of the author's recorded vocal performance of the texts. This is one, relatively familiar, way in which the piece sounds the silence of spelt air. Its most significant algorithmic exploration of sounding is, however, the excavation and redistribution of paraphones. These are taken from one text to be added to the other, and vice versa. Words from one text that 'spell out' phonemes from the other interrupt and arbitrarily, silently sound full words in their companion text. The processes are documented in live-coding notebooks: one that builds and serves the animations in real time; another that contains preliminary studies and some exposition; and one with algorithms which generate the texts-to-be-read by extracting and distributing phonemic paragrams, i.e. paraphones.
instructions: To experience the piece as envisioned and as inwardly evocalized by the author – in terms of temporality and rhythm – please follow the link provided, opting for full screen if at all possible. The animated text is intended to be read as it presents itself, any without reader transaction. If you refresh the page, random entry points into the work will result, for the juxtaposed texts in both columns.

The work manipulates paraphones; sounds from one text are integrated into the other, causing silent interruptions that form new words. The creation process is thoroughly documented in live-coding notebooks, which present the animations in real-time and include preliminary studies and algorithms for redistributing these phonemic paragrams to generate the final texts.

title: Crawl It's Image
descriptionOfWork: Crawl It's Image is a bilingual paragrammic reading of - and writing with - Samuel Beckett's «l'Image», a constituent passage of his last novel. This novel, Comment c'est, was composed in French and translated by Beckett himself as How It Is. 'Grams' from twenty-two paragraphs of the original French are excavated from within the words of the novel's English text. The animation of Crawl It's Image reveals and highlights these 'literal grams' of the French. Adjacent English words contain them and 'define' the French words. Between these definitive collocations, the artist has added Beckettian phraseology to render the resultant constrained surface narrative a little more hospitable and, most certainly, more 'how it is.'
instructions: The animation of Crawl It's Image proceeds without transaction. One complete cycle of this animation takes about forty-seven minutes. If you are viewing the piece on a device that you control, you may 'hover' over certain parts of the screen. Hover over the upper register in order to reveal credits and links to supporting material, or hover over the displayed paragraph, to highlight all of its letteral French grams.   Letting the animation proceed without triggering these features is the artist-intended experience. In this more passive mode, you may nonetheless read in at least three ways. You may read each screen as you would any other such 'page' of text. You may follow the leading word of the animation: If you do this, you will be reading in time with the artist's own vocal performance of the English composition. Or you may read the animation for the highlighted French letteral grams, following, more slowly, the original text of Beckett's "l'Image."

title: Undead Computer
descriptionOfWork: "Undead Computer" is an example of one of the most fundamental units of storytelling: it is simply a premise. It implies many things (among them, a mystery about what killed the computer and what its memory or data-collection has retained from the experience of being dead) and those are available to the audience to speculate on or modify.
instructions: The website "undead.computer" contains one challenge, which is to respond to a certain prompt with the name of the thirteenth month ("Persephone") , and after that, it is simply a calendar, navigable by the arrow keys, each day of which has a space for a poem in the style of Edgar Lee Masters' Spoon River Anthology, so that the audience can supply their own take on what a machine-object would report of itself from beyond its own demise. Email the.undead.computer@gmail.com according to instructions found under any available (vacant) date on Persephone's calendar. Remember that this is only a premise, and represents something in pre-development, an idea in a nascent stage, and so as a game, while there is a way to "succeed" at finding the Calendar, there isn't a quest or objective as such unless the audience creates one collectively (and eventually) by deciding on the elements of a mystery (or some other 'winnable' experience) and their providing clues to their solutions in their creative writing. Even when complete, the final product would represent a 'zero draft', something yet to be focused into a single, sharp, actionable design idea. .

title: Indexing the Index
descriptionOfWork: Based on a corpus comprised of the indexes of 3 books (Updating to Remain the Same: Habitual New Media | Wendy Hui Kyong Chun, Code and Clay, Data and Dirt: Five Thousand Years of Urban Media | Shannon Christine Mattern, and The Moment of Complexity: Emerging Network Culture | Mark C. Taylor) selected by the artist from the Cybernetics Library's 'Uncomputable' collection, the generator produces speculative indexes, using Natural Language Processing techniques to map textual data spatially. This ongoing project explores the index as a creative infrastructure for mapping knowledge and associative relationships within information.  The system generates unique spatial layouts of text on the page, where each index entry's horizontal position is determined by its semantic proximity to others in the dataset (as determined by an approximate nearest neighbors algorithm), forming a multiply-determined visual topology of relationships.   The webpage provides a visual and textual interface to explore a dataset of index entries and their associated metadata. An interactive 3D t-SNE visualization displays the vector space, each point representing an index entry. Users can generate a new speculative index by clicking a button, which highlights the corresponding selected entries in the visualization, constructing a unique shape each time it is regenerated.

curatorialStatement: The Index Generator, based on indexes from three selected books, creates speculative indexes using Natural Language Processing to spatially map textual data. By generating new indexes, users see unique spatial layouts and semantic proximities within the dataset, providing insights into the interconnectedness of information.

descriptionOfWork: "Go To Sea" is a retro pixel narrative game that immerses players in the transformative era of 1990s China, a period characterized by rapid privatization and modernization. Set in a northern Chinese industrial town, the game centers around the story of Xiao Kang, a young man employed at a neighborhood bathhouse. This communal space acts as a nexus for local residents to congregate, share stories, and exchange information, gradually influencing Xiao Kang's thoughts and worldview.  Inspired by the personal experiences of the game's creators, who spent their formative years in small cities across mainland China during the late 80s and early 90s, "Go To Sea" endeavors to encapsulate the essence of the "run to Xiaokang" - the pursuit of a Moderately Prosperous Society. This concept, initially proposed in 1979, envisioned a society with a thriving middle class, but it also gave rise to internal conflicts and emotional deprivation amidst the backdrop of material abundance.  Through a genre-crossing narrative woven with loosely connected scenes, "Go To Sea" intertwines the independent yet interconnected storylines of multiple characters. The game meticulously recreates the familiar streets, food stalls, TV channels, and books that shaped the creators' shared collective memories and the experiences of those around them. By presenting players with a relatable yet thought-provoking journey, "Go To Sea" delves into the challenges and struggles individuals face as they navigate the unprecedented forces of modernization in China.  As the team's first foray into traditional narrative gaming, "Go To Sea" represents a departure from their previous focus on simulations and computational projects. Through moments of violence, loss, sadness, day-passing, happiness, and excitement, the game reflects the hardships and triumphs of its characters, inviting players to embark on a sincere journey that captures the realities of rapid modernization and the lingering sense of loss, sadness, and anger that defined a generation.

The game, inspired by the creators' experiences, explores the pursuit of a moderately prosperous society and its associated conflicts. Through interconnected character stories, players navigate scenes that reflect the cultural and societal changes of the era. It offers a thought-provoking journey into the challenges of modernization.

title: i cannot go
descriptionOfWork: i cannot go is a webpage of shuffle poetry as an exploration of everything I love about new advances in technology / accessibility: the ability to experiment and play with the framework, a platform to save and show the work, and, most of all, an invite to interact with the code instead of simply pressing a button or dragging and dropping. As much as I love WYSIWYG drag-and-drop, I'm most satisfied with tweaking every element myself (and solving the problems I end up causing). i cannot go uses the perchance.org framework, HTML/CSS styling, black-and-white images, and randomly compiled human-generated language. It evolves in full title and content both as I periodically add to it and as the observer interacts with it. For example: the nonsense-text is obscured in the poem itself and cannot be read on the webpage, but copy and paste it into a textbox or search bar and it will be revealed. This is one of a few more subtle interactions that can be found by spending time with the work itself. As for the poetry; it's about nostalgia. It's about places we've been, places you've been, places I've been, and how hard it is to leave those places without permission from someone else. (Who is this someone else? That's up to you.) It's about wondering how breathing and grief and crying and waking up smiling all fit together. It's about how much of a liminal space any given public bathroom can be when empty. It's about how sometimes people don't care, and you have to keep going. It's about how many words I can fit on the page before it stops making sense.

The work evolves as the creator adds to it and as users interact with it, highlighting the dynamic nature of digital poetry.

title: Ultra-Large: Impossible worlds
descriptionOfWork: An interactive versions of my Ultra-Large Visual Narrative worlds built through a collaborative AI process and exploring the intersection of machine and organic, the mix of human-made and more-than-human creatures. Using the generative powers of AI outpainting, and starting the process with my own work, I build expansive, evolving and large visual worlds, with stories hidden throughout them. Overall, my goal is not to replicate existing art practices, but instead to find new pathways for digital writers and attempt to build new creative forms and processes through what's possible and what's impossible with machine learning and generative AI. These large imaginary worlds will then be transformed into exploratory game spaces. Readers/users can explore those spaces and experience the stories, narratives and poetry embedded within them. How this happens is via an automatically generated poetic analysis of each Ultra-Large visual world.  Poetic text is then loaded on to the image, as are diagrams, lines and other markers indicative of the analysis.  The result is a strange automatic experience, where these Ultra-Large worlds spin past the reader, forever being dissected and re-thought, broken apart into spots and moments and visual targets.   The poetic texts are further broken down into reverse. They were generated by human, but the human then generates AI code for those texts.  It's a strange cycle of make and unmake, between two systems, electric and electrically organic.  Playing and Reading is simple,  let is generate, pause to read, unpause to continue generating.
instructions: Simple.  Wait for loading and generating. Then let the work run/think.  Press Pause to stop and read. Unpause it to continue generating. Pause again to read. And on and on it goes.

creatorBiography:
Patrick Lichty is a multifaceted artist known for his work in various media. Born in Akron, Ohio, in 1962, Lichty's upbringing was immersed in art, and science fiction. His career spans over three decades, during which he has established himself as a media artist, writer, curator, designer, and educator. Lichty's artistic practice primarily focuses on exploring the impact of media on society and individual perception. He has a particular interest in augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), artificial intelligence (AI), and non-fungible tokens (NFTs). His work critically examines how media culture shapes human perceptions of reality, particularly at the intersection of the virtual and physical worlds.

He is especially recognized for his contributions as a principal member of the virtual reality performance art group Second Front and as the animator for the activist group The Yes Men. His diverse skills in digital intermedia include proficiency in printmaking, kinetics, video production, generative music, and neon art. Additionally, Lichty's role as a media "reality" artist and theorist reflects his deep engagement with how media and mediation influence our understanding of the environment.

Apart from his artistic endeavors, Lichty has also made significant contributions as an educator and holds a position at Winona State University. His accolades include being a CalArts/Herb Alpert Fellow and an exhibitor at the Whitney Biennial.
title: Studio Visits: In the Posthuman Atelier
descriptionOfWork: A conceptual exhibition catalogue artwork that documents an exhibition in which a human curator "visits" 50 synthetic AI artists (note that all the chairs are empty, and the floors are clean)  This project conceptually accesses the anxieties of AI-based image generation, its relation to Benjamin's "Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction", the author's ideas on "The Culture of "Like"", and the coming of the "Psychosis of Representation".  Over a 4-month period, (from August 2022) the artist used MidJourney v4 to create uncannily realistic art studios, then generated artist's names/statements using GPT3. The only thing that is not generated is the curatorial statement.  The project is a Picasso-esque "Lie which reveals the Truth."
genreKeywords: Narrative, Conceptual, Literary, Non-interactive, Machine Learning
curatorialStatement: Studio Visits AI explores the intersection of AI and art through a speculative project featuring 50 synthetic artists. Utilizing platforms like MidjourneyAI and ChatGPT-3, it generates studio portraits and artist statements, questioning the future relevance of human creativity in the arts. The project critically engages with digital art anxieties, highlighting the impact of AI on artistic practices. It reflects on the potential revolution AI could bring to the art world, presenting a purely AI-driven exhibition curated by a human.

title: Reality Shows
descriptionOfWork: In times of constant crisis there is an urgent need for innovative forms of writing that can adequately represent the complexities of the current climate emergency. Traditional narratives often struggle to convey the multifaceted nature of climate change, which involves a multitude of interconnected actors enmeshed with one another across vastly variable scales of time and space. This proposal seeks to explore how hypermedia fiction, with its capacity to create linkages between disparate elements, can serve as a platform for representing these intricate interactions. By leveraging the unique capabilities of hypermedia, we can develop a more comprehensive understanding of the interconnected nature of this complex issue and its wide-ranging implications.  REALITY SHOWS is a hypertext that follows a dystopian reality show franchise as a way to confront the entangled nature of spectacle, globalization, neocolonialism, and climate justice in the Anthropocene. The project seeks to challenge traditional boundaries and power structures, and to highlight the realities that aren't typically shown on camera.  The narrative is generated by a system of actor-based models that simulate the intertwined interactions between contestants, viewers, corporations, the weather, and the built environment. By giving agency to both human and non-human intelligences, the project seeks to reflect the complex interdependencies that characterize our world. The results of these simulations are then inputted into a generative AI, which outputs the data as natural text that is then formatted into a web-based hypertext. The resulting narrative embraces the chimeric nature of existence, a narrative re-wilding that invites us to imagine new ways of being where the lines between technology, ecology, and society are blurred and redrawn in ways that open up new possibilities for living on this planet.
instructions: The narrative of REALITY SHOWS unfolds in a non-linear fashion by clicking links to navigate to different pages. These links are highlighted in blue. The web-based hypertext also supports bi-directional links. Backlinks to notes linking to the current note are found in the sidebar. Pages and their links are also shown as an interactive graph at the bottom of the page. Clicking on a node will navigate the user to that particular page.
genreKeywords: Hypertext, Narrative, Generative, Literary, Combinatorial, Interactive fiction
curatorialStatement: Reality Shows is a hypermedia fiction project addressing the climate emergency through a dystopian reality show narrative. It explores themes of spectacle, globalization, neocolonialism, and climate justice. The story is generated using actor-based models and generative AI to simulate interactions between contestants, viewers, corporations, weather, and the built environment. This approach highlights the interconnected nature of our world, blurring lines between technology, ecology, and society. An early prototype features 25 events and 5 agent types.
