title: Throughlines: An (Un)Linked Hypertext Poem
descriptionOfWork: “Throughlines" is a poem and a tool for poem creation. It is a meditation on human / computer cognition and materiality. The poem's text explores these ideas using language that both evokes the supposed ephemerality and the inextricable materiality of the digital. Leveraging the affordances of the Twine Editor, it invites the reader to not only select between links but to establish links themselves. Twine projects can be opened in the browser for reading or playing but also can be imported into the editor itself. The reader draws the links between pre-written lines of poetry, creating an associative poem that resonates with the work of Vannevar Bush and N. Katherine Hayles through both its text and its links.
instructions: "Throughlines" is a poem read in the Twine Editor. To engage with it, import the attached Throughlines.html as a story. The "Import" option is inside the "Library" tab. You will see some passages. The "Start" passage includes a short description of the piece and brief instructions. Passages A-Z are lines of poetry pre-written by the author. You can create links between these lines using the following syntax: [[Words to click on->Destination passage]] For example, to create a link between the word "emulate" in passage C that links to passage D, you would wrap the word "emulate" like so: [[emulate->D]] You can see your poem at any time using the "Play" button under the "Build" tab. You can change the starting pass by selecting the passage of your choice and clicking "Start Story Here" on the Twine toolbar. When you are finished, export your poem as an .html file using the "Publish to Story" option under the "Build" tab.
genreKeywords: Hypertext, Participatory, Conceptual, Poetry, Combinatorial
curatorialStatement: Throughlines quite literally asks the reader to become a collaborator in constructing its poetry, by instructing them to download and edit the work's original Twine source file. Participant poets find text therein that they must link together to form verse, using the OG creator's words and their own mental connections to co-write the final work. The work itself explores ephemerality and digital materiality, human cognition and association, and the human connectivity created through digital tools.

creatorBiography: As an Environmental Humanities graduate student, my research and creative interests revolve around ecological ways of being, as informed by posthumanism and daoism, and its cultivation via entertainment media and play. I graduated from Yale-NUS College with a BA (Hons) in Psychology, and have been exploring other methodologies alongside empirical research, from ecocriticism to ethnography.
title: Unnamed: a Nature Poem?
geographicalOriginOfWork: Australia, China, Singapore, Switzerland, United States
descriptionOfWork: Our conception of nature as the flip side of the artificial/human/technology is the source of our divergence from ecological balance. Paradoxically, in trying to create clear boundaries around nature to rescue it, we further distance it. Daoism encapsulates this duality — that which can be named is not the eternal name; the former illuminates its manifestations (the illusion of distinct bodies), and the latter reveals its mysteries (our inscrutable entanglement as its patterns) - but both link to harmony and understanding.  Hypertext, in its disruption of traditional notions of linearity and the dichotomy of a clear input and output, source and reference, object and sign, serves as a means for expressing the performativity of posthumanism. In this Daoist meditation on nature, I attempt to engage in a more broadly construed practice of hypertextualization, in blurring the boundaries between poetry, cinematography, music, nature, truth, and expression. However, try as I might to suspend the impulse to name, demarcate, and categorize through blurring foreground and background via playful language, improvisational music, and cinematic stillness, I ultimately fail to escape the meaning-making that falsely distances nature. In my attempt however, I have thankfully shed more certainty. I hope that in encountering my work, the audience too, is led into the deeper mystery.  My creative process was intentionally nonlinear, and I tried to follow my embodied impulses and avoid over intellectualizing. I alternated writing poetry and music in a call and response to each other. I felt like the essence of the piece was still far from my goal of unnaming nature, so I elected to add a visual component to further decenter my presence. I selected old clips and filmed new footage based on how they related to, evoked, or challenged what was in the composition so far. I experimented with different video transitions but settled on a simple crossfade to further soften boundaries and mimic the poetics of the spoken component without introducing any distractions. I used an exponential fade to similarly blend sounds from the clips, with attention to how they would intersect with the music. Another effect I heavily used was the warp stabilizer to eliminate camera movement to give the impression of environments that exist vibrantly even without the presence of an observer.
instructions: You are invited to join me in this attempt to unname — to delay foreclosure, to stay with the trouble, to consider how you are symptomatic everchanging fiber of a deeper mystery.
genreKeywords: Hypertext, Narrative, Conceptual, Poetry, Literary, Cinema, Combinatorial
curatorialStatement: Unnamed: a Nature Poem? explores the paradox of defining nature, suggesting that doing so distances us from ecological balance. It uses Daoist principles and hypertext to blur boundaries between various forms of art and nature, aiming to reveal deeper connections. The creative process is nonlinear, blending poetry, music, and visuals to soften distinctions and highlight the intertwined nature of existence. The work invites the audience to embrace mystery and shed certainty, reflecting on our relationship with nature and technology.

title: Deformance as Un/linking
descriptionOfWork: This exhibition explores deformance as a radical (un)linking from the pre-existing source text in shifts of media, form, and intention. Four deformances of literary works underlines "the theoretical commonality that holds their practices of "deformance", that is, the "deforming and performing anew" of past literary and artistic texts (Prescott; Samuels and McGann, 25).   Jolene Armstrong's "Spelarne"- published in Swedish 1903, is a protomodernist short story by Hjalmar Soderberg. This "deformance" argues through a re-imagination of the story through layers from text to illustration to abstraction and then finally to augmented reality, feeding lines of text to various generative AI and through hand drawn and printed imagery, to create a textual experience that deforms and oscillates to moving picture, revealing the way in which Soderberg was anticipating a modernist manner of writing for cinema.   Kari Maaren's "Moor and Mead Hall" "deforms" the opening of the Anglo-Saxon epic Beowulf by presenting it as music. Reducing Beowulf from words to music reveals the underlying tension the poet frames as a battle between the justified Danes and the monsters abandoned by God, identifying it as an issue of territory, not morality. By removing the voice of the poet and leaving sound alone, "Moor and Mead Hall" focuses on the story beneath the Christian filter that itself may initially have deformed the oral pre-Christian version of the epic.  Siobhan O'Flynn's "An Experiment in Yellow: 'THE YELLOW WALLLPAPER. THE YELLOW WALLPWAPER. The lyelorwwalplater"' is a digital "deformance" in Twine of Gilman's short story "The Yellow Wallpaper" (1892), remediating passages of text through multiple cycles of prompts between Midjourney, ChatGPT, and DALL-E. "An Experiment in Yellow" "deforms and performs" the story anew to underscore the collapse of meaning-making into chaos in generative AI's successive self-cannibalizing remediations. The intention is to amplify the unease rippling through the spiraling destabilization of the protagonist's consciousness while also asking what is the literary? How integral is humanity to authorship and how can that be defined? The interactor can decide.  Monique Tschofen's "In There Behind the Door" is a digital deformance of Gertrude Stein's Tender Buttons (1914) that makes visible her "topopoetics" (Cresswell). This work, published in Scalar, tests sound-, text-, image-, and video-generating AI-tools where arguably "there is no there there"--to iteratively reveal her poetics as a dense intertextual crossroads where operational pronouns of place mash up Aristotelian, Baconian, and Cartesian topoi together with Matisse's "Grand Interieur Rouge."

Monique Tschofen’s digital deformance of Tender Buttons uncovers its intricate intertextuality. Each project creatively blends text, visuals, and sound, challenging traditional interpretations and inviting fresh perspectives.

title: What did the line that you last drew ask you?
descriptionOfWork: What did the line that you last drew, ask you?,' presents a virtual platform for digital exhibition and performance. This work is a research collaboration between Alys Longley, Jeffrey Holdaway and Kate Stevenson of DotDot Creative Studio, made in collaboration with international artists (such as pavleheidler [Sweden], Francisco González Castro [Chile], val smith [NZ] ). The DotDot Social platform offers a new form of virtual performance space that combines live interaction with artwork online. We will present an interconnected series of virtual worlds that cross creative disciplines from contemporary poetics, performance, choreography, sound composition, gaming and visual art. Our site is highly interactive and is constantly iterating in relation to audience feedback.  Our virtual platform curates and translates artworks into interactive immersive worlds through visual imaginings, creating playful interactive spaces within the worlds, and finding ways in which the site can be simultaneously a performance, an exhibition, an installation, a repository for creative process and a space where contributions from audiences can be held.  Participants enter the digital exhibition 'What did the line that you last drew ask you?' via a simple button, and meet inside the digital exhibition/performance together. They can then converse in real time, while being able to see each other through real-time avatars accessing the microphone and camera of their device, and navigate through a series of digital worlds or rooms, navigable via the different studio research projects that inform this work. The resources of digital gaming, real-time social connection and virtual interactivity, are brought together in a series of experiments in poetry, choreography and visual art.

creatorBiography:
Annie Grosshans is a lifelong multidisciplinarian with a core affinity for text-based expression. Working in communities of visual art, publication, performance, video/film and now the cyber, she's explored the expressive opportunities of her era giving voice to the oft-incongruent selves surfacing from her experience. This exploration from the beginning has been informed by and centered in feminist thinking, both practical and theoretic.

Throughout a time of tsunamic, cross-cultural change, she has used her creative practice as the fulcrum for discovering & giving form to the meaning of our connectivity.

She brings her experiences and the understandings gleaned from them to the creative project before us now of conceiving and living a realigned conception of ourselves with one another and the earth.

title: ThinkingDaughters
descriptionOfWork: I and my collaborator composed ThinkingDaughters into the code as we built the site.  The content was influenced by the capabilities and demands of the digital language, which in turn influenced the presentational form of the work. There are eight main vertical screens, each progressing the narrative with the downward scroll.  Lateral screens open off each of the main screens to elaborate on the meanings broached by the verticals. Horizontally to the right are "Authortorials," lyrical expressions built from events in the author's life and from her generation (aging and passing away) born into social change and argument over what constitutes the life and purpose of a woman. Horizontally to the left are "Narratorials," excerpts from the writings of "AncestressPrintLiterates," women writers foundational to the author's thinking. There is an associative meaning and directionality between quotations, as well as to the overall narrative flow of work.   ThinkingDaughters employs a multiplicity of "voices": poetic, expository, directed to the reader and self-focused; presented as on-screen text and/or as audio and video. The thematic core of the work centers on the question of what is literacy, now, as its carrier and custodian transmutes from print to the still evolving, socially entangled cyber tool and medium? How can this tool help us recognize and culturally integrate the exponential growth in research and human expression emerging from the subjectivity and selfhood spoken by and for our/themselves, powered by revelatory understandings centered on gender, race, class, country and language of origin?  This deepening knowledge offers realignment of our relational structures as we live under the shadow of an environmental reckoning which, ThinkingDaughters argues, could give reason for human recognition of our connectivity with all life and this Earth.
instructions: Please view this iteration of ThinkingDaughters by maximizing the web browser window on a 1080p display.  The main navigational tool is the SPINEOFTELLINGS table of contents that is always present near the upper left side of all screens of the site. Navigation for the main vertical screens is done with arrows at top and bottom of the center spine of each screen or by scrolling the page.  Horizontal navigation of the Narratorials and Authortorials is done by the Narratorial / Authortorial bar at the bottom of each screen. Underlined text and all text with arrows are clickable, including the Narratorial "Germinations" and "What Inspired".  Clicking the dots menu of the BookScans will change the image. In the Authortorials, clicking on "ReadMore" will expand the text to the next sentence.  Clicking on the "Remember" text on the main screens ToGrowAGirl and OurAncientArguments presents videos.
